A documentation team is preparing a careful catalogue for readers who have never visited its collection. Each record must distinguish the name of an item from its description, the purpose of the current question, and the evidence used to support an answer. The team keeps the original spelling so that later readers can check the source without guessing what an editor intended. A short answer is useful only when it addresses the requested distinction. Extra comments about appearance, location, ownership, or price should not replace the requested classification.

During review, two editors read every record independently. They compare ordinary usage, note possible ambiguities, and retain disagreements rather than silently changing the observations. Their notes explain that an unfamiliar name is not evidence that an item belongs to a different group. Likewise, a familiar name does not remove the need to read the question. Records are organised into separate sections, but the position of a record is an administrative choice and is not part of its meaning. Nothing in the preceding discussion supplies the answer for the particular entry below.

For the final entry, use the ordinary concrete meaning of the name. Do not treat it as a company, a surname, a metaphor, or a software command. Give the requested common category rather than repeating the name. The review form accepts a concise category word; explanations can be written in a separate document. The entry and the question follow this background so that the answer can depend on all information that has actually been supplied.

For guava, supply the ordinary category rather than a description of the individual item.
